chapters.title: The dragon's defeat leads into continued danger while testimony explains the saints' victory
chapters.summary: A woman clothed with the sun cries out in labor. A great red dragon with seven heads waits to devour her child. Her son, who will rule the nations, is caught up to God. The woman flees to the wilderness. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him down to the earth. A voice calls him the accuser and says the brothers overcame him. The dragon pursues the woman, and the earth helps her. He goes to make war on the rest of her offspring.
chapters.meaning: Verses 7–9 show the dragon thrown out of heaven by Michael. Verse 10 calls him the accuser of the brothers. Verse 11 says how the brothers themselves overcame him. Two means are named: the Lamb’s blood and the word of their testimony. They did not love their life, even to death. So their victory does not mean they were spared. Verse 12 confirms it: the dragon comes down in great wrath.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects this victory with testimony and the Lamb's blood. How can continued earthly danger occur within the account of the dragon's defeat?

chapters.historicalNote: The woman and dragon appear as signs, so their features require reading within the vision. The child's rescue frustrates the dragon before the woman receives nourishment in a prepared wilderness. Michael's battle removes the accuser's heavenly place rather than ending every danger on earth. The announced victory rests on the Lamb's blood and testimony held under threat of death. The dragon's remaining fury then targets the woman and her other offspring. Earthly suffering can continue within the account of victory without proving that rescue has failed.

chapters.title: Worship becomes coercion when deceptive signs and economic exclusion support the beast's power
chapters.summary: A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads. The dragon gives it power, and one head has a healed death wound. The whole earth marvels and worships it. It speaks blasphemies and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb. It works signs and makes people worship the first beast’s image. It puts a mark on the right hand or forehead of all. The number of the beast is 666.
chapters.meaning: Verses 13–15 show the second beast using signs and the threat of death. Verses 16–17 add a quieter pressure. Everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, receives a mark. Verse 17 states its use: no one can buy or sell without it. Worship is thus enforced through the market. Verse 10 has already told the saints what this requires: endurance and faith. Verse 18 calls for wisdom about the number.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson compares the dragon's methods with the Lamb's response. How does control over buying and selling turn worship into coercion?

chapters.historicalNote: The first beast receives the dragon's authority and attracts wonder through its healed wound. That wonder becomes worship, while its granted power turns against the saints. The second beast resembles a lamb but speaks like a dragon, joining appearance with deception. Its signs support an image whose worship is enforced through threat of death. The mark then makes buying and selling depend on participation, connecting worship with economic pressure. The number calls for understanding without securely naming a present person or technology.

chapters.title: Following the Lamb contrasts with enforced worship while harvest images announce judgment
chapters.summary: John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name. They sing a new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. An angel flies with eternal good news for every nation. A second says Babylon has fallen. A third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath. A voice blesses the dead who die in the Lord. One like a son of man reaps the earth’s harvest. An angel gathers the grapes and throws them into the winepress of God’s wrath.
chapters.meaning: Chapter 13 showed worship of the beast enforced by a mark. Verses 9–11 warn what that worship leads to. Verse 12 turns to the saints and names what the moment asks: perseverance. It describes them by two things they keep. They keep God’s commandments, and they keep the faith of Jesus. Verse 13 adds a blessing for those who die in the Lord. They rest from their labors, and their works follow them.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects the angel's gospel with Restoration teaching and shared participation. How does following the Lamb differ from the beast's enforced worship?

Angels call every people toward the Creator while announcing Babylon's fall and opposing beast worship. The blessing on faithful dead answers pressure by naming rest and works that follow them. Harvest and wine-press images then present judgment through gathering and violent separation. The chapter preserves that severity while locating endurance in keeping God's commands and Jesus' faith.

chapters.title: The victors' song praises just rule before the final plagues leave the heavenly temple
chapters.summary: John sees seven angels with the seven last plagues. Those who overcame the beast stand on a sea of glass mixed with fire. They hold harps of God. They sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb. The song says all nations will come and worship. The temple of the tabernacle of the testimony opens in heaven. One of the living creatures gives the angels seven golden bowls of wrath. Smoke fills the temple, and no one can enter until the plagues end.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 says the last plagues complete God’s wrath. Before they fall, verse 2 shows the victors standing by a sea. Verse 3 names their song after Moses and after the Lamb. Israel sang with Moses beside the sea after its rescue (Exodus 15:1). The words praise God’s works as great and his ways as righteous and true. Verse 4 adds that all nations will come and worship. So the judgments that follow are introduced as just.

lds.text: Why does the victors' song appear before the final plagues?

Their song joins Moses with the Lamb, connecting rescue with praise rather than personal achievement. The words identify God's ways as righteous and anticipate worship from all nations. Angels then emerge from the heavenly temple with the bowls of wrath. Smoke from divine glory prevents entry until that sequence reaches completion. Worship frames approaching judgment without claiming that its destructive scenes are gentle or incidental.

chapters.title: Repeated refusal of repentance interrupts the bowls with a warning to remain alert
chapters.summary: A voice tells the seven angels to pour out the bowls. Sores, a sea of blood, and rivers of blood follow. The sun scorches people, and they blaspheme and do not repent. The beast’s kingdom is darkened. The Euphrates dries up for the kings from the east. Three unclean spirits like frogs gather the kings for war. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying, “It is done,” and a great earthquake. Great hail falls, and people blaspheme God.
chapters.meaning: Verses 9 and 11 report twice that people did not repent. Verses 13–14 show spirits gathering kings for war. Verse 15 breaks into the account in the first person. The speaker says he comes like a thief. No time is given, so the instruction is to watch. The blessing is for one who stays awake and keeps his clothes. Verse 16 then returns to the gathering of the kings.

lds.text: What does the warning about alertness require when it gives no date?

chapters.historicalNote: The bowls extend damage from marked worshipers into waters, heat, and the beast's darkened kingdom. The angel's explanation connects blood-filled waters with blood that the persecutors themselves poured out. Yet sufferers answer with blasphemy rather than repentance, continuing the failure named after earlier trumpets. Deceptive spirits then gather kings through signs for war, while a warning calls for alertness. The unexpected-coming comparison addresses conduct without supplying a calculated calendar. The final bowl declares completion amid shaking and Babylon's remembered wrongdoing, leaving symbolic geography unassigned.

chapters.title: The city's powerful partners become agents of its ruin rather than a secure protection
chapters.summary: An angel shows John a woman seated on a scarlet beast. She wears purple and gold and is drunk with the saints’ blood. Her name is “Babylon the Great.” The angel explains the mystery. The beast’s seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings. The ten horns are ten kings who give their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and he will overcome them. The horns will hate the woman, the great city, and burn her.
chapters.meaning: Verses 12–13 describe ten kings who give their power to the beast. Verse 14 states their aim and its outcome in one sentence. They make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb overcomes them. The reason is his rank: Lord of lords and King of kings. The verse also names those with him: called, chosen, and faithful. Verse 16 then shows the same kings turning on the woman. Verse 17 says God put this into their hearts.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson reads Babylon as a warning against the world's wickedness. How do the city's supporting rulers become agents of its destruction?

chapters.historicalNote: The woman rides a beast and displays costly clothing, jewels, and a golden cup. Her drunkenness with the saints' blood connects that splendor with violence rather than innocent wealth. The angel explains waters, heads, and horns as peoples and rulers within the vision. Those rulers unite behind the beast, but their war cannot overcome the Lamb. They then turn against the very woman whose position appeared to depend on their support. Shared destructive power becomes unstable without supplying a secure list of historical or modern kings.

contextNote.title: The city's powerful partners become agents of its ruin rather than a secure protection
contextNote.text: Verses 12–13 describe ten kings who give their power to the beast. Verse 14 states their aim and its outcome in one sentence. They make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb overcomes them. The reason is his rank: Lord of lords and King of kings. The verse also names those with him: called, chosen, and faithful. Verse 16 then shows the same kings turning on the woman. Verse 17 says God put this into their hearts.

chapters.title: The city's trade and violence explain why departure must mean refusing participation
chapters.summary: An angel cries that Babylon the great has fallen. Another voice calls God’s people to come out of her. Her sins have reached heaven, and she will be repaid double. Kings who shared her luxury weep at the smoke of her burning. Merchants weep because no one buys their cargo. The list runs from gold and spices to the bodies and souls of people. Shipmasters cry out that such wealth was ruined in one hour. A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, and the city’s music stops.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 says nations, kings, and merchants all shared in the city’s wealth. Verse 4 speaks to a different group: “my people.” They are told to come out of her. Two reasons are given. They must not share in her sins, and they must not receive her plagues. The cargo list shows what sharing would mean. It ends in verse 13 with people’s bodies and souls.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects departure from Babylon with refusing participation in wrongdoing. Why does leaving the city require refusing participation in its wrongdoing?

chapters.historicalNote: Babylon's fall introduces a command to leave so that God's people avoid participation in wrongdoing. The repeated laments come from kings, merchants, and sailors whose wealth depended on her luxury. Their distance expresses fear of torment rather than care for those harmed by her power. The merchandise list includes human bodies and souls, exposing people within the trade as goods. Lost music, work, light, and weddings make the city's disappearance affect its whole ordinary life. The ending names bloodshed, giving judgment a cause beyond the mere existence of wealth.

chapters.title: Wedding joy and the rider's judgment replace the city's splendor and deceptive rule
chapters.summary: A great crowd in heaven praises God for judging the great prostitute. A voice announces the Lamb’s marriage, and his wife has made herself ready. John falls to worship the angel and is told to worship God. Heaven opens, and a rider called Faithful and True sits on a white horse. His robe is sprinkled with blood, and his name is the Word of God. A sword comes from his mouth. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire. The birds are called to feed on the armies.
chapters.meaning: Verse 7 says the Lamb’s wife has made herself ready. Verse 8 describes her clothing: bright, pure, fine linen. Two phrases explain it. “It was given to her” makes the clothing a gift. The linen is also “the righteous acts of the saints.” The verse holds both without choosing. The woman of 17:4 wore purple, scarlet, gold, and pearls.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects this vision with preparation for the Second Coming. How does wedding clothing differ from the city's purchased splendor?

chapters.historicalNote: Heavenly praise answers Babylon's fall by naming judgment as true and righteous. The wedding clothing receives explanation as the saints' righteous acts rather than purchased luxury. John must not worship the announcing servant, preserving the distinction between a messenger and God. The rider called Faithful and True then judges through the sword proceeding from his mouth. The beast and false prophet lose the power whose signs supported forced worship. The violent supper contrasts with the wedding invitation, keeping rescue and judgment distinct.

chapters.title: Bound deception and final judgment deny death and power their last claim over the dead
chapters.summary: An angel binds the dragon in the abyss for a thousand years. Those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus live and reign with Christ. This is called the first resurrection. After the thousand years Satan is released and gathers Gog and Magog. Fire devours them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. John sees a great white throne. The dead are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.
chapters.meaning: Verse 11 shows a great white throne, and earth and sky flee from it. Verse 12 shows who stands there: the dead, “the great and the small.” Rank gives no shelter. Two kinds of book are opened. The books record works, and the dead are judged by them. The other is the book of life. Verse 13 adds that the sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects opened books with final judgment and present choices. How does judgment of great and small limit the apparent protection of power?

chapters.historicalNote: Binding the dragon interrupts his deception, while killed witnesses receive life and share Christ's reign. The vision distinguishes that first resurrection from the later raising of the remaining dead. Released deception briefly gathers nations again before their attack ends through fire from heaven. The final throne then brings great and small together before opened books. Judgment according to works removes the protection that rank or power might seem to offer. Death and Hades enter the fire, so their custody of the dead cannot remain final.

chapters.title: God's dwelling brings renewed life while the holy city reverses the earlier account of luxury
chapters.summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea is no more. The holy city, new Jerusalem, comes down from God like a bride. A voice says God’s dwelling is with people. The one on the throne says he is making all things new. An angel shows John the city, with twelve gates named for Israel’s tribes. Its twelve foundations bear the names of the Lamb’s apostles. The city is pure gold, and its gates are pearls. It has no temple or sun, for God and the Lamb light it.
chapters.meaning: Verse 3 announces that God will live with people. Verse 4 says what his presence removes. He wipes every tear, as 7:17 promised. Then four things end: death, mourning, crying, and pain. The verse gives the reason: “The first things have passed away.” The book has shown those first things in its seals, trumpets, and bowls. Verse 5 answers them with one sentence from the throne: all things new.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson reads these promises through the hope of celestial glory. How does the descending city answer earlier accounts of loss and exploitation?

chapters.historicalNote: The holy city descends from God rather than becoming a destination reached through human conquest. The promised dwelling removes death, mourning, and pain, answering losses named throughout the earlier visions. Carey reads the descending city as renewed shared life rather than escape from the world. The city's measured beauty belongs to the Lamb's bride rather than Babylon's wealth through exploitation. No temple is needed because God and the Lamb supply presence directly. Open gates and light for nations describe welcome, while exclusion preserves truth and purity.

chapters.title: The river and tree make life available while the final invitation requires faithful hearing
chapters.summary: The angel shows John the river of life flowing from the throne. The tree of life grows beside it, and its leaves heal the nations. God’s servants will see his face, and there will be no night. Jesus says he is coming soon. John falls before the angel and is again told to worship God. He is told not to seal the book, for the time is near. A warning forbids adding to or taking from the book’s words. The book ends with a prayer for the Lord Jesus to come.
chapters.meaning: Verse 1 shows the river of the water of life, and verse 2 the tree. Verse 17 turns the vision into an invitation. The Spirit and the bride say “Come.” Each hearer is told to pass the word on. Then the thirsty are invited, and the water is free. In 21:6 the one on the throne made the same offer. Chapter 18 showed a city where everything had a price.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects the opening river and light promises with celestial glory. How do freely offered water and faithful hearing belong together in the final invitation?

chapters.historicalNote: Water proceeds from the throne, and the tree's leaves serve the healing of nations. Removed curse and direct sight of God's face answer earlier separation, threat, and loss. John again receives a correction against worshiping the messenger rather than God. The repeated coming promise leads into conduct and reward without providing a calendar for readers. The invitation offers water freely, while warnings protect this prophecy from additions and removals. Prayer and grace return the visions to assemblies who must hear, keep, and await.

contextGuide.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Different messages test endurance and conduct without making earlier faithfulness sufficient
steps.text: Verses 2–3 praise Ephesus for work, endurance, and testing false apostles. Verse 4 still holds one thing against it: it left its first love. Verse 5 gives three commands in order. Remember where you fell from, repent, and do the first works. Past labor does not replace them. The warning is concrete: the lampstand will be moved from its place. In 1:20 a lampstand is an assembly, so the assembly itself is at risk.

steps.title: The slain Lamb's worthiness changes grief into shared praise and hope of redeemed life
steps.text: Verse 4 shows John weeping because no one can open the book. Verse 5 announces a Lion, and verse 6 shows a slain Lamb. The song in verse 9 says why this Lamb is worthy. The reason is not strength: “for you were killed.” His blood bought people for God. They come from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Verse 10 adds what they become: a kingdom and priests.

steps.title: Worship becomes coercion when deceptive signs and economic exclusion support the beast's power
steps.text: Verses 13–15 show the second beast using signs and the threat of death. Verses 16–17 add a quieter pressure. Everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, receives a mark. Verse 17 states its use: no one can buy or sell without it. Worship is thus enforced through the market. Verse 10 has already told the saints what this requires: endurance and faith. Verse 18 calls for wisdom about the number.
